title: A B1 SINE element within the mouse Malat1 long noncoding RNA acts as an internal ribosome entry site mediating micropeptide translation.
abstract: In most cells, Malat1 long noncoding RNA localizes to the nucleus where it affects splicing and chromatin function. In mouse neurons, Malat1 is exported to the cytoplasm where it is translated to generate the M1 micropeptide. Here, we characterize an internal ribosome entry site (IRES) required for M1 translation that is sufficient to induce cap-independent expression of a downstream open reading frame. In vivo chemical probing and structural modeling defined a three-stem-loop RNA secondary structure that encompasses the active IRES segment and coincides with a mouse B1 SINE (short interspersed element) repetitive element. In affinity purification experiments, a minimal IRES/B1 RNA selectively bound ribosomal subunits, translation factors, and the known IRES cofactors Rack1 and hnRNP A2/B1. Depletion of Rack1 and hnRNP A2/B1 inhibited IRES-dependent translation of the reporter and expression of the endogenous M1 peptide. Our study identifies an unexpected functional unit hidden within a widely studied long noncoding RNA.

title: The isolated HEPN domain of SACSIN exhibits RNA-binding activity.
abstract: Autosomal Recessive Spastic Ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (ARSACS) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by mutations in the SACS gene, though the molecular function of its protein product, SACSIN, remains elusive. Therapeutic strategies for ARSACS are limited, mostly due to the exceptionally large size of SACSIN (~ 520 kDa), which precludes conventional gene therapy and standard molecular delivery methods. Over 200 pathogenic variants, including missense, nonsense and frameshift mutations, have been identified. Regardless of variant type, patients uniformly exhibit cerebellar ataxia, spasticity and peripheral neuropathy. Among them, patients with homozygous frameshift or missense mutations within the SACSIN higher eukaryotes and prokaryotes nucleotide-binding (HEPN) domain, suggesting that the alteration of the functional role of the SACSIN HEPN domain could be linked to the manifestation of ARSACS symptoms. Here, we show that the SACSIN HEPN domain can bind RNA in overexpression, corroborating the hypothesis that SACSIN functions as an RNA-binding protein. The interaction of the SACSIN HEPN domain with the RNA regulates the cellular compartmentalization of this domain as well as its propensity to form protein condensates. Conversely, an ARSACS mutated version of the SACSIN HEPN domain (F4574C) showed an impaired RNA-binding activity, a nuclear mis-localization and the predisposition to form protein condensates. Overall, our study unveils an unknown molecular function of the SACSIN HEPN domain that, if formally confirmed also for the full-length SACSIN, can pave the way for innovative therapeutic approaches for ARSACS patients.

title: Variant escape site mapping and characterization of SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid rapid antigen test antibodies.
abstract: Rapid antigen tests (RATs) were a critical tool for diagnosing severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection during the height of the pandemic, but their performance depends on antibodies that remain robust to viral evolution. Since most commercial RATs target the viral nucleocapsid protein, mutations in this domain can compromise binding and test performance. To systematically define this risk, we used deep mutational scanning (DMS) to map escape mutations for 82 antibodies across 43 commercially available tests, generating the most comprehensive escape database of SARS-CoV-2 viral mutations to date. Most antibodies target conformational epitopes, with 47 (57%) mapping to the RNA-binding domain and 23 (28%) to the dimerization domain. Principal component analysis and clustering revealed escape phenotypes, including shared features outside of predicted epitopes. As the pandemic proceeded, we noted a change in industry preference from IgG to IgM-type antibodies, which was associated with changes to epitope sub-class prevalence. Analysis of paired capture-detection antibodies revealed a preference for targeting the same structural domain (20/33 or 61%), indicating a slight preference for test antibodies to hit orthogonal yet proximal sites. Together, the results establish a comprehensive resource for understanding how SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein mutations affect antibody binding and the phenotypes that underlie RAT antibody selection. This resource and approach can help prioritize antibodies for follow-up performance testing and support the design of more mutation-resilient diagnostics.IMPORTANCEIt is critical during a pandemic for diagnostic tests to be accurate and for the false negative rate to be kept low. The rapidly changing nature of SARS-CoV-2 exposed a weakness with using rapid antigen tests to diagnose infection, as mutations to the viral nucleocapsid protein can cause the virus to evade detection. In this work, we systematically tested the robustness of 82 antibodies from 43 separate commercially available tests by deliberately mutating the nucleocapsid protein and investigating which changes caused weakened binding to the test antibodies. In addition to determining which specific tests were at risk from certain mutations, we collated our datasets into a meta-analysis, allowing us to identify some best practices for designing robust tests. We, therefore, expect that this resource will support the design of more mutation-resilient diagnostics, whether for future variants of SARS-CoV-2 or in applying these principles to other respiratory viruses, such as influenza virus.

title: Reliability of Machine Learning Approaches Towards the Identification of Novel PI4KIIIβ Inhibitors.
abstract: The type III Phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase (PI4KIIIβ) serves as a key host factor that mediates the replication of RNA viruses and is involved in essential membrane trafficking events. The development of PI4KIIIβ-specific inhibitors could give insights into the enzyme's function and contribute to the treatment of viral diseases. However, the molecular features that determine inhibitor activity and selectivity remain unclear. PI4KIIIβ inhibitors with reported biological activities (pIC50) were systematically analyzed using machine-learning methods. Molecular characterization was performed using RDKit, Chemopy descriptors, and PubChem fingerprints. Multiple classification and regression models were developed and evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation to establish robust structureactivity relationships. It was suggested that the PubChem fingerprint-based linear regression, SMOreg, and GaussianProcesses models were more appropriate for the studied dataset to deliver the best predictive ability, which showed a correlation coefficient value > 0.7 in the 10-fold crossvalidation. PubChemFP389 and PubChemFP572, representing amidine-like fragments or guanidine- related motifs, and the aromatic amine fragment showed a negative correlation with respect to biological activity. The study describes predictive models and provides insights into essential structural features in chemical compounds relevant for inhibitory activity, which could assist in the design and optimization of novel PI4KIIIβ inhibitors for antiviral and anticancer applications. A similar approach may be extended to a larger dataset of molecules or to other related drug targets. The findings suggest that excessive basicity and certain polar functionalities may be detrimental to PI4KIIIβ inhibition, providing important insights into the structural features influencing ligand binding and activity.

title: Circular RNAs in cancer: from biomarkers to vaccine-based immunotherapy.
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are endogenous, covalently closed RNA molecules generated through back-splicing that exhibit exceptional stability, evolutionary conservation, tissue-specific expression and diverse regulatory functions. Compared with conventional RNA-based therapeutic platforms, such as messenger RNAs (mRNAs), small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), microRNAs (miRNAs), and long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), circRNAs offer enhanced resistance to exonuclease-mediated degradation, prolonged intracellular persistence, and sustained protein expression. These characteristics have positioned circRNAs as promising candidates for cancer biomarkers and next-generation therapeutic platforms. Recent evidence indicates that they regulate multiple biological processes associated with tumour initiation and progression, including transcriptional regulation, miRNA sequestration, RNA-binding protein modulation, alternative splicing, cap-independent translation, immune signalling, and therapeutic resistance. Through interactions with innate and adaptive immune pathways, circRNAs regulate antigen presentation, cytokine production, immune-cell activation and tumour immune evasion, highlighting their importance in cancer immunotherapy. This review summarizes recent advances in circRNA biogenesis and their roles in cancer progression, therapeutic resistance, and immune regulation, with particular emphasis on engineered circRNAs as platforms for cancer vaccines and precision immunotherapy. We discuss advances in circRNA vaccine design, delivery, neoantigen targeting, biomarkers, and clinical translation, while highlighting key challenges including manufacturing, immunogenicity, tumor heterogeneity, regulatory requirements, and limited clinical validation. Overall, circRNAs represent a promising and versatile platform for cancer immunotherapy, with continued advances in RNA engineering, personalized neoantigen design, targeted delivery, and clinical evaluation expected to determine their potential for translation into effective and durable cancer treatments.

title: Opsonic Peptide MOP3 Attenuates Ischemic Acute Kidney Injury.
abstract: Renal ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) induced acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and serious condition characterized by renal dysfunction, inflammation, tubular injury, and cell death. Extracellular cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (eCIRP) is a damage-associated molecular pattern that contributes to inflammation and tissue injury. MFG-E8-derived oligopeptide 3 (MOP3) is an opsonic peptide that binds eCIRP and promotes its phagocytic clearance. Here, we investigated the therapeutic effects of MOP3 in a murine model of renal I/R-induced AKI. Mice were subjected to 30 minutes of bilateral renal ischemia and treated with MOP3 or vehicle at the onset of reperfusion. Blood and kidney tissues were collected 20 h later. Renal inflammation, kidney function, tubular injury markers, histological damage, and cell death were assessed by RT-qPCR, biochemical assays, Western blotting, hematoxylin and eosin staining, and TUNEL staining. MOP3 treatment reduced circulating eCIRP by 40% and renal IL-6, IL-1β, MIP-2, and KC mRNA expression by 43%, 84%, 73%, and 69%, respectively, compared with vehicle treatment. Serum urea nitrogen, creatinine, and NGAL levels were reduced by 56%, 63%, and 44%, respectively, after MOP3 treatment. MOP3 also decreased renal KIM-1 and NGAL mRNA expression by 88% and 44% and reduced their protein levels by 29% and 45%, respectively. Furthermore, MOP3 attenuated renal tubular injury and decreased TUNEL-positive cells. These findings demonstrate that MOP3 attenuates inflammation, renal dysfunction, tubular injury, and cell death following renal I/R, suggesting that MOP3 may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for ischemic AKI.

title: miR-142-3p overexpression targets CLTA and impairs clathrin-mediated endocytosis in HLSECs induced by high glucose.
abstract: This study aims to explore the effect of miR-142-3p on the endocytosis in human liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (HLSECs) induced by high glucose and to investigate the underlying mechanisms. Multi-database target prediction was performed to identify potential targets of hsa-miR-142-3p. HLSECs were cultured under 5.5 mmol/L glucose (normal) or 25 mmol/L glucose (high) conditions. qRT-PCR assessed the RNA expression levels of miR-142-3p and CLTA. Western blot assessed the protein expression levels of clathrin-mediated endocytosis(CME)-related genes. Immunofluorescence assay was used to observe the cellular localization of CLTA. A dual-luciferase assay investigated the targeting relationship between miR-142-3p and CLTA. DiI-LDL endocytosis assay was used to study the endocytosis in HLSECs. Bioinformatics analysis predicted CLTA as a potential target of miR-142-3p. The expression level of miR-142-3p was increased and the expression levels of CLTA, α-adaptin, AP2M1 and VPS35 were reduced in high glucose-induced HLSECs (P < 0.05). DiI-LDL endocytosis assay demonstrated that the endocytosis was weakend in HLSECs induced by high glucose. Dual-luciferase reporter assay confirmed that miR-142-3p directly targets CLTA. Compared with the negative control group, inhibition of miR-142-3p significantly increased the expression levels of CLTA, AP2M1, α-adaptin and VPS35, and improved the endocytosis in HLSECs (P < 0.05). In contrast, overexpression of miR-142-3p showed the opposite effects. miR-142-3p overexpression targets CLTA and impairs CME in HLSECs induced by high glucose. The concurrent changes in other CME-related genes further suggest a broader regulatory role of miR-142-3p on the endocytosis.

title: WSSV355 enhances IDH1 enzymatic activity and promotes efficient WSSV replication.
abstract: White spot syndrome virus (WSSV) drives extensive metabolic reprogramming to support viral replication, including activation of reductive carboxylation, a pathway in which host isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 (IDH1) has a central role. However, the mechanisms by which viral factors regulate IDH1 and associated metabolic networks remain unclear. Here, we identified WSSV355 as a key viral regulator that contributed to IDH1 binding and activation during infection. Using yeast two-hybrid screening, WSSV355 was identified as an LvIDH1-interacting protein and further validated by co-immunoprecipitation and co-localization analyses. Functional assays demonstrated that WSSV355 enhanced IDH1 enzymatic activity, whereas truncation mapping revealed that distinct regions of WSSV355 contributed to IDH1 binding and activation. In vivo silencing of WSSV355 suppressed viral gene expression, and decreased viral genome copy number, establishing its role in promoting efficient WSSV replication. Affinity purification-mass spectrometry (AP-MS) further revealed that WSSV355 identified a set/network of WSSV355-associated proteins enriched in cytoskeletal, RNA-processing, and metabolic pathways. Integration with infection-responsive proteomic datasets identified candidate modules linking the WSSV355-associated protein network to host infection responses, suggesting broader potential involvement of WSSV355 in host cellular processes during infection. Collectively, these findings identify WSSV355 as an LvIDH1-interacting viral protein that enhances IDH1 enzymatic activity and is required for efficient WSSV replication. To our knowledge, WSSV355 is the first reported virus-encoded protein shown to enhance IDH1 enzymatic activity, providing new insights into how aquatic viruses exploit host metabolic machinery to promote infection.

title: SYNPRED: A Synergistic Approach to Multimodal Learning for Clinical Prediction
abstract: Multimodal medical data captures complementary aspects of disease. It provides a comprehensive basis for diagnosis and the identification of biological associations linked to progression or treatment response. Established contrastive learning approaches exploit shared information across modalities, but fall short in exploiting complementary, modality-specific signals relevant for a task. Here, we propose a synergistic multimodal variational autoencoder (VAE) framework that separates task-relevant unimodal and multimodal information from instance-specific variation task-irrelevant, allowing complementary signals across modalities to be leveraged for prediction. The method yields benefits even if modalities are missing at test time. We evaluate the method on a treatment response prediction task using medical imaging and RNA data. Empirical comparison with alignment-based and multimodal VAE state-of-the-art approaches demonstrates improved multimodal prediction performance, and consistent benefits for prediction from a single modality after multimodal training. The full code can be found here: https://github.com/cirmuw/SYNPRED.

title: Non-canonical cleavage expands prime editing in 5' direction
abstract: Cleavage-dependent CRISPR-Cas gene editing relies on RNA-guided DNA cleavage that drives cellular machinery to incorporate intended edits. Beyond canonical cleavage, CRISPR nucleases can also execute non-canonical cleavage on the displaced DNA strand. Here, we report a modified design principle for prime editing that leverages the non-canonical cleavage activity, enabling editing in the 5' direction of a classic nick site. We elucidate the non-canonical-cleavage-driven reverse transcription pathway that initiates upstream of the classic nick site. We identify competition between the canonical and non-canonical routes, which can be modulated by rationally designing RNA templates carrying the intended edits. We demonstrate that cellular physiology enhances editing efficiency from individual reverse-transcription product yet exerts limited influence on pathway competitions. Our findings revise the design principle of prime editing and establish a new dimension for engineering CRISPR-Cas systems by harnessing its intrinsic, non-host-specific, non-canonical cleavage activity.

title: Alterations of SLC14A1 mRNA structure are frequently detected in weak Jka presenting donors.
abstract: RNA structural changes caused by mis-splicing or transcription errors may affect antigenic features of cell surface proteins. They are especially noteworthy in the field of blood transfusion where the discrepancy between DNA-based molecular testing and serological blood typing are often encountered in clinical practice and lead to mismatched blood transfusion. In the Kidd (JK) blood group system weak Jka (Jk(a + w)) phenotype is usually missed in routine serological tests and causes delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions. However molecular bases underlying Jk(a + w) phenotype are still not clear although plentiful genomic DNA-based studies have been conducted. In this study, we used PacBio long-read sequencing to characterize open reading frame (ORF) region of SLC14A1 mRNA obtained from reticulocytes of 18 blood donors possessing JK*A alleles. Among them, 8 donors were determined as normal Jka antigen presentation and 10 donors showed Jk(a + w) phenotype in routine serological tests. We found that Jk(a + w) subjects demonstrated different exon combination patterns compared to those individuals presenting normal Jka antigens, implying the resulted SLC14A1 protein isoforms could make different contributions to the formation of the JK antigenicity. Moreover, exon skipping and exon inclusion that were frequently found in Jk(a + w) individuals could induce frameshift mutations. In addition, high levels of nucleotide insertions or deletions (indels) at 130A position were detected in the transcripts of Jk(a + w) individuals. Technical artifacts were examined using synthesized RNA templates and the results suggested that artifacts generated in reverse transcription and PCR amplification (RT-PCR) processes were unlikely the causes of these observations. All the results indicate that SLC14A1 RNA splicing and transcription fidelity play crucial roles in determining Jka antigen presentation.

title: Botrytis virus X ORF2 suppresses RNA silencing in a trigger-restricted manner and is associated with altered Dicer-like gene expression in Botrytis cinerea.
abstract: RNA interference (RNAi) is a central antiviral defence mechanism in fungi, yet relatively few mycoviral suppressors of RNA silencing (VSRs) have been functionally characterized, particularly in phytopathogenic hosts. Botrytis virus X (BVX), a positive-sense RNA virus in the family Alphaflexiviridae, infects Botrytis cinerea and encodes five predicted ORFs, most of which have unknown functions. Here, we screened BVX ORFs 2-5 for RNA silencing suppressor activity using complementary GFP-based assays in Nicotiana benthamiana and examined the leading candidate in the fungal host B. cinerea. BVX ORF2 (X2) enhanced GFP transcript and protein accumulation in assays where silencing was triggered by sense RNA but failed to suppress silencing triggered by hairpin-derived small interfering RNAs or microRNA-guided targeting, indicating a trigger-restricted suppressor phenotype. In B. cinerea, transgenic expression of X2 was associated with reduced induction of the RNAi-associated genes BcDCL1 and BcDCL2 compared with empty-vector controls, with the strongest effect observed on BcDCL1. In a virus-infected fungal background, X2 expression was also associated with increased viral RNA accumulation. Together, these results identify BVX X2 as a BVX-encoded, trigger-restricted suppressor of RNA silencing and link its expression to altered RNAi-related gene induction and increased viral RNA accumulation in B. cinerea.

title: Single-Particle Deconvolution of Electroporation Artifacts Guides the Rational Engineering of CD47-EV-Liposome Hybrids for siRNA Delivery.
abstract: The clinical translation of small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapeutics is hampered by the lack of efficient delivery systems. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) hold great promise as natural carriers, yet conventional loading methods, most notably electroporation, suffer from low encapsulation efficiency, structural damage, and poorly characterized aggregation artifacts. Using single-particle nano-flow cytometry, we deconvoluted these electroporation-induced artifacts and revealed that true loading efficiency is only ∼24%. To overcome these limitations, we engineered CD47-functionalized EV-liposome hybrid vesicles via membrane fusion of CD47-overexpressing EVs with siRNA-loaded liposomes. The hybrid design integrates the high payload capacity of synthetic liposomes with the intrinsic biocompatibility and immune-evasive functionality of CD47-engineered EVs. In a Transwell coculture model simulating the competitive uptake environment of the tumor microenvironment, the hybrid vesicles evaded macrophage clearance and delivered anti-PD-L1 siRNA to tumor cells, resulting in ∼60% PD-L1 gene silencing, three times that of electroporation (∼20%). By providing a rationally designed hybrid nanocarrier with validated immune-evasive and RNAi performance, this work offers a significant advancement for EV-based RNA interference (RNAi) therapeutics.

title: SMART Nanocarriers for siRNA Delivery: Stimuli-Responsive Platforms for Targeted Gene Silencing.
abstract: Despite the remarkable specificity of small interfering RNA (siRNA)-based treatments for gene silencing, biological limitations like poor stability, rapid systemic clearance, immunogenicity, and inefficient intracellular delivery hinder their clinical translation. A promising strategy for overcoming these challenges and enabling precise, site-specific gene silencing is the use of SMART nanocarriers, including stimuli-responsive, adaptable, and multifunctional delivery platforms. Controlled siRNA release, enhanced cellular uptake, and effective endosomal escape are enabled by these novel nanocarriers' ability to respond dynamically to exogenous triggers such as light, ultrasound, and magnetic fields as well as endogenous stimuli such as pH gradients, redox potential, enzymatic activity, and hypoxia. Recent advances have combined rational material design, surface functionalization with targeted ligands, and modular architectures to gain spatiotemporal control over gene silencing while limiting unintended targets and systemic toxicity. This study examines the critical design concepts, fabrication methodologies, and molecular pathways governing SMART nanocarrier-mediated siRNA distribution, with a focus on polymeric, lipid-based, inorganic, and bioinspired platforms. The article highlights key preclinical and emerging clinical breakthroughs, as well as issues with scalability, repeatability, immunocompatibility, and regulatory translation. This review emphasizes the critical significance of stimulus-responsive nanocarriers in developing siRNA treatments towards precision medicine applications in oncology, neurological disorders, and inflammatory illnesses by consolidating recent studies and future prospects.

title: Anatomically Accessible Local mRNA Therapeutics: From Anatomical Access to Disease-Focused Applications.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics have expanded from clinically validated prophylactic vaccines toward protein replacement and supplementation. Yet mRNA delivery remains centered on intramuscular vaccination and intravenous administration, largely optimized for systemic adaptive immunity or circulation-mediated biodistribution. Many localized diseases, however, are confined to tissues or compartments accessible by topical, transdermal, inhaled, oral, catheter-based, ocular, or intra-articular administration without initial reliance on circulation. For these diseases, the therapeutic objective is likewise local: therapeutically relevant mRNA expression occurs within the affected tissue, and efficacy derives predominantly from the local biological activity of the encoded protein rather than from downstream systemic effects initiated by local expression. This therapeutic paradigm is defined here as Anatomically Accessible Local mRNA Therapeutics (ALmT). The review first distinguishes ALmT from intravenous mRNA delivery and intramuscular mRNA vaccination, then organizes site-specific barriers and engineering strategies across major anatomical sites. It further examines disease-focused ALmT applications, highlighting protein restoration, cytokine or growth-factor supplementation, local antibody-fragment production, regenerative modulation, and tissue repair. Finally, it discusses general design principles, quantitative PK/PD evaluation, repeat-dose safety, and clinical translation. Overall, the ALmT framework may facilitate the design, quantitative evaluation, and clinical translation of mRNA therapies for localized diseases.

title: MERS-CoV accessory ORF proteins in innate immune evasion: an evidence-graded functional framework.
abstract: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) is a merbecovirus associated with recurrent zoonotic spillover and severe lower-respiratory disease. Research has focused largely on DPP4-mediated entry, spike structure, replicase biology, neutralizing antibodies, and vaccines. However, the 3'-encoded accessory proteins are increasingly recognized as context-dependent modulators of viral fitness and pathogenesis. ORF4a binds double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) and suppresses MDA5- and PKR-dependent antiviral responses; ORF4b antagonizes OAS-RNase L and NF-κB signaling and contributes to inflammatory pathology in defined infection models; ORF5 modulates interferon and inflammatory responses in a genetic-background-dependent manner; and ORF8b interferes with MDA5- and HSP70-IKKϵ-dependent signaling, although its pathogenesis phenotype varies by experimental system and viral background. ORF3 shows HUWE1-regulated pro-apoptotic activity in ectopic-expression systems, but its role during authentic MERS-CoV infection remains unresolved. Our review organizes these findings by evidence type, pathway position, cell or tissue context, sampling time, and genetic-interaction evidence. This framework separates demonstrated mechanisms from inferred biological consequences and identifies the validation required before accessory-ORF biology can inform host-range assessment, therapeutic development, sequence surveillance, or rational attenuation.

title: High-order chromatin structures mediated by phase separation in cell senescence.
abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) coordinates biomolecular condensates to establish three-dimensional chromatin architecture and epigenetic regulation. The progressive loss of epigenetic information is a fundamental, reversible driver of cellular senescence. In this review, we systematically synthesize emerging evidence on the spatiotemporal dynamics of LLPS-mediated chromatin compartmentalization during the aging process. We highlight how age-dependent alterations in histone, RNA, and DNA modifications disrupt multivalent interactions, leading to constitutive heterochromatin dissolution, aberrant transcriptional condensate formation, and nucleolar expansion. Furthermore, biomolecular condensates undergo age-dependent biophysical maturation-shifting from dynamic liquid states to solid-like aggregates-which dictates structural chromatin erosion and topologically associating domain (TAD) fusion. These diverse biophysical defects can be consolidated within a unified "condensatopathy" framework, encompassing both loss-of-function failures and toxic gain-of-function protein aggregations across somatic aging, stem cell exhaustion, and neurodegeneration. Understanding how phase separation regulates higher-order chromatin structures provides profound insights into aging trajectories. Ultimately, selectively modulating the material properties of biomolecular condensates, rather than merely dissolving them, offers a transformative precision therapeutic paradigm to restore epigenetic fidelity and counteract age-related diseases.

title: Correction: RNA binding motif protein RBM41 promotes colorectal tumorigenesis by impeding the maturation of NDRG1 pre-mRNA.
[Mechanism of gypenoside LI inducing apoptosis and autophagy in clear cell renal cell carcinoma cells via ROS/JNK and Akt/mTOR signaling pathways].
abstract: This study aims to investigate the anti-proliferative effect and molecular mechanism of gypenoside LI(Gyp LI) in clear cell renal cell carcinoma(ccRCC) and elucidate its regulatory effect on apoptosis, autophagy, reactive oxygen species(ROS) signals, and related pathways. The effect of Gyp LI on ccRCC cell viability, proliferation, apoptosis, autophagy, and migratory capability was observed and assessed by cell counting kit-8(CCK-8), colony formation test, flow cytometry, Hoechst staining, wound healing assay, and transmission electron microscope(TEM). RNA sequencing, gene set enrichment analysis(GSEA), and Western blot were used to identify and verify the signaling pathways involved. The results show that Gyp LI significantly inhibits the proliferation of ACHN cells and 769-P cells, with IC_(50) values of 72. 30 and 62. 57 μmol·L~(-1) after treatment for 48 hours. Meanwhile, Gyp LI induced nuclear pyknosis and karyorrhexis, inhibited colony formation and cell migration, upregulated the expressions of B-cell lymphoma-2 associated X protein(Bax), cysteinyl aspartate-specific proteinase-3(caspase-3), microtubule-associated protein 1A/1B-light chain 3(LC3)-Ⅱ/LC3-Ⅰ, autophagy-related protein 5( ATG5), phosphorylated c-Jun n-terminal kinase( p-JNK), and phosphorylated p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase( p-p38 MAPK), downregulating the expressions of B-cell lymphoma-2( Bcl-2), sequestosome 1(p62), phosphorylated protein kinase B(p-Akt), and phosphorylated mammalian target of rapamycin(p-mTOR). Mechanistically, Gyp LI activated c-Jun N-terminal kinase( JNK)/p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase( p38 MAPK) pathways, inhibited protein kinase B(Akt)/mammalian target of rapamycin(mTOR) pathways, and promoted autophagy in ccRCC cells. Autophagy inhibition further enhanced apoptosis. Gyp LI also markedly induced ROS production, and this effect was partially reversed by N-acetyl-Lcysteine(NAC). Subcutaneous xenograft experiments of ACHN cells in BALB/c nude mice demonstrate that gypenosides can safely and effectively inhibit tumor growth. In conclusion, Gyp LI exerts anti-ccRCC effects by coordinately regulating ROS-mediated stress signaling, mitochondrial apoptosis, and autophagy.

title: Defects in ribosomes and translational control in lymphoid leukemia and lymphoma.
abstract: Translational control has emerged as a critical layer of gene expression reprogramming in cancer, with the ribosome functioning as a central regulatory node rather than a passive protein synthesis machinery. This review provides an integrated overview of how defects in ribosomes and translational regulation contribute to the pathogenesis of lymphoid leukemias and lymphomas. We focus on 3 major axes: mutations in ribosomal proteins, alterations in ribosomal RNA, and dysregulation of translation initiation mediated by the eukaryotic initiation factor 4F complex. Recurrent mutations in ribosomal proteins, such as RPL10 in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and RPS15 in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, alter ribosome function, leading to selective changes in mRNA translation, impaired translational fidelity, and increased oxidative stress that promotes genomic instability. In parallel, emerging evidence indicates that alterations in ribosomal RNA, including changes in ribosomal DNA copy number, biogenesis, and epigenetic modifications, contribute to ribosome heterogeneity and oncogenic transformation, although their precise roles in hematologic malignancies remain incompletely understood. Furthermore, aberrant activation of translation initiation pathways-often driven by the AKT/mTOR/MYC signaling axis-enhances both global protein synthesis and selective translation of oncogenic transcripts, reinforcing malignant phenotypes. Together, these ribosome-intrinsic and -extrinsic defects converge to reprogram the translatome, promote tumor progression, and create therapeutic vulnerabilities. Targeting translational control mechanisms therefore represents a promising strategy for the treatment of lymphoid malignancies.

title: Physicochemical properties, in vitro digestive behavior, and fecal fermentation characteristics of a polysaccharide fraction from Triadica rotundifolia.
abstract: In this study, a polysaccharide fraction from Triadica rotundifolia (formerly Sapium rotundifolium Hemsl.), designated RSP, was obtained by hot-water extraction, ethanol precipitation, Sevag deproteinization, and sequential chromatographic purification. Its physicochemical characteristics, simulated digestive behavior, and effects on human fecal microbiota were systematically evaluated. RSP was obtained at a yield of 1.21%, and high-performance gel permeation chromatography (HPGPC) showed a dominant chromatographic peak with a weight-average molecular weight (Mw) of 322,357 Da. RSP exhibited a distinct monosaccharide composition, with arabinose, glucuronic acid, galactose, and glucose as the major monosaccharides. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and atomic force microscopy (AFM) further revealed typical polysaccharide functional groups and an aggregated, irregular morphological organization. During simulated gastrointestinal digestion, reducing-sugar equivalents changed only slightly during the salivary and gastric phases but increased markedly during the intestinal phase. The presence of RSP during in vitro fecal fermentation resulted in notable alterations in culture turbidity, progressive acidification, relative SCFA profiles, and microbial community structure. Furthermore, 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing revealed distinct fecal microbial community profiles among the RSP, Blank, and INU groups. In the LEfSe multigroup comparison, Bifidobacterium was identified as one of the taxa characterizing the RSP group. Collectively, these findings provide an integrated characterization of the physicochemical properties, in vitro digestive behavior, and fecal fermentation characteristics of RSP.

title: MaltEms-MaltOBP9 axis mediates sexually dimorphic olfactory behavior in Monochamus alternatus via recognition of pheromone 2-methoxy-4-vinylphenol.
abstract: The olfactory system is essential for insect survival and behavior, with odorant-binding proteins (OBPs) playing a key role by binding and transporting chemical signals to olfactory receptors. Although MaltOBP9 from Monochamus alternatus, a primary vector of pine wilt disease, has been linked to olfactory functions in M. alternatus, its regulatory mechanisms and specific roles are not well understood. In this study, we show that MaltOBP9 is highly expressed in the antennae of both male and female adults after sexual maturation. Using fluorescence spectroscopy, molecular docking, and site-directed mutagenesis, we identified the amino acid Phe54 as essential for MaltOBP9's ability to bind 18 different volatile compounds. RNA interference (RNAi) and behavioral tests revealed that MaltOBP9 is necessary for sexually mature adults to detect the pheromone 2-methoxy-4-vinylphenol (2M4VP). Additionally, dual-luciferase reporter assays, electrophoretic mobility shift assays, and RNAi experiments demonstrated that the transcription factor MaltEms positively regulates MaltOBP9 expression, thereby influencing the detection of 2M4VP. By combining insights into transcriptional regulation and protein-ligand interactions, this study clarifies the MaltEms-MaltOBP9-2M4VP axis as a mediator of sex-specific olfactory behavior-where females avoid and males are attracted to the pheromone-in sexually mature M. alternatus. These findings provide a theoretical basis for developing pest control methods that target MaltOBP9 and its critical residue Phe54 through behavior-based strategies.

title: DNAJC17 regulates RNA splicing in auditory hair cells and is required for hearing.
abstract: RNA splicing is essential for gene regulation, but its role in maintaining cochlear hair cell function remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify a heterozygous missense variant (c.401A>C, p.E134A) in DNAJC17, which encodes a spliceosome-associated protein, that segregates with adult-onset progressive hearing loss in a multigenerational family. Hair cell-specific deletion of Dnajc17 in mice results in profound deafness with progressive hair cell degeneration, establishing its essential role in cochlear maintenance. Hair cells lacking DNAJC17 exhibit marked stereocilia disorganization accompanied by widespread alternative splicing defects in the cochlea. Notably, the dual-specificity protein kinase Clk1 that regulates pre-mRNA splicing shows altered exon inclusion, consistent with disruption of splicing control networks. In addition, Dnajc17 p.E134A knock-in mice develop adult-onset progressive hearing loss with stereocilia and mitochondrial abnormalities but preserve hair cell survival, recapitulating the human phenotype. Together, these findings identify DNAJC17 as a causative gene for autosomal dominant hearing loss and identify RNA splicing regulation as a key mechanism required for long-term maintenance of cochlear hair cell integrity.

title: Structural basis and rational engineering of a thermophilic Cas13a for robust RNA detection.
abstract: Cas13a enzymes are particularly attractive for nucleic acid detection due to their robust collateral activity. Recently, there has been a surge in the discovery and engineering of thermostable Cas13a proteins for nucleic acid detection. The thermostable Cas13a from Thermoclostridium caenicola (TccCas13a) was identified; however, its native target sensitivity and collateral activity are relatively low and require optimization for molecular diagnostic applications. Here, we report comprehensive biochemical characterization and structure-guided engineering of TccCas13a. Our analyses reveal its intrinsic thermostability, nucleotide substrate preferences, and tolerance to structured target RNA substrates. Rational engineering of the spacer-target RNA binding channel improved target engagement and enabled determination of a 3.13 Å cryo-electron microscopy ternary structure. Furthermore, extensive structure-guided engineering of active site-proximal regions yielded a variant with over ∼100-fold enhanced target sensitivity and collateral activity across diverse biological matrices. Together, our work provides mechanistic insights and establishes TccCas13a as a platform for next-generation RNA diagnostics.

title: Reverse transcribed ssDNA derepresses translation of a retron antiviral protein.
abstract: Retrons are bacterial immune systems that prevent phage propagation by initiating a toxic response within infected hosts. Previously characterized retrons produce abundant multicopy single-stranded DNA (msDNA) by reverse transcription, which acts as an antitoxin in the absence of phage. However, we describe here a non-canonical mechanism for type VI retrons, which do not produce detectable msDNA in the absence of phage yet still provide defense. Focusing on Retron-Vpa2 from V. parahaemolyticus, we show broad defense against phages and identify triggers of the system when expressed in E. coli. Within the retron operon, we find a highly enriched, structured transcript that we term a hybrid RNA (hyRNA). The hyRNA contains the reverse transcription template and a toxin coding sequence that is repressed by a riboregulator. In our model of triggering, phage infection induces accumulation of msDNA, which hybridizes to the riboregulator and enables RNase H cleavage, derepressing translation of the toxin.

title: Chemically tailored lipids mediate solid-phase RNA programming of mineralized microenvironments.
abstract: The localized delivery of RNA therapeutics to mineralized tissue interfaces is limited by poor retention and rapid clearance at the target site. We report the development of a solid-phase transfection platform that functionalizes mineralized surfaces into bioactive nucleic acid reservoirs. Through the rational design and screening of a library of 21 piperazine-linked bisphosphonate ionizable lipids, we identified a lead formulation of bisphosphonate lipid nanoparticle (BP-LNP) that maximizes hydroxyapatite affinity without compromising transfection potency. Upon adsorption onto mineral substrates, these BP-LNPs resisted fluid removal and maintained surface-mediated, sustained delivery of encapsulated RNA cargo to adjacent cells. We demonstrated the versatility of this Mineralized Tissue-Targeting Expression System (MiTEX) composed of BP-LNPs in two therapeutic contexts: Cre recombinase mRNA-functionalized allogeneic bone grafts to genetically label de novo bone formation in vivo, and STAT3 siRNA delivery to reduce inflammation in human gingival explants. This platform provides a universal strategy for transforming inert calcium phosphate materials and tissues into locally bioactive RNA delivery systems for regenerative and immunomodulatory applications.

title: Repurposing Type III CRISPR-Cas as Modular Cellular RNA Biosensors.
abstract: Over the past decade, CRISPR-Cas based biosensors have emerged as sensitive, specific and programmable platforms for nucleic acid detection, with applications ranging from diagnostic tools, environmental monitoring and various applications in fundamental research. The vast majority of these biosensors are currently limited to in vitro applications, highlighting the need for cellular platforms. Here, we provide a perspective on the potential of type III CRISPR-Cas systems as a platform for real-time RNA biosensing in living cells. We discuss the unique properties that distinguish type III from other CRISPR-Cas types, including their intrinsic cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) signal amplification cascade, PAM-free RNA targeting and the extensive biochemical diversity of their downstream CARF and SAVED effector proteins. We outline the fundamental design principles of a genetically encoded type III cellular biosensor, comprising a programmable guide RNA, a multi-subunit sensing complex and a cOA-sensing effector protein capable of generating optical or electrochemical readout signals. A remaining challenge for type III cellular biosensors is the inherent cytotoxicity of canonical cOA-activated effectors. We propose several strategies to re-engineer these outputs towards non-cytotoxic reporter systems. While cellular biosensors present a natural route toward in vivo sensing, they face many challenges beyond the choice of the output signal and hardware strategy. We conclude that type III CRISPR-Cas is a promising platform for programmable real-time RNA sensing in living cells, utilizing its diverse modular effector outputs, representing a significant expansion of the CRISPR biosensor toolkit, while emphasizing appropriate deployment scenarios that enables full potential of these biosensors.

title: HIV-1 hijacks HGF/c-MET signaling to promote viral entry and replication in primary CD4+ T cells.
abstract: The mesenchymal-epithelial transition factor (c-MET) is a receptor tyrosine kinase best known for mediating hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) signaling in cancer, but its role in HIV-1 infection has remained unclear. Here, we identify c-MET as a host factor that promotes HIV-1 replication in CD4+ T cells by facilitating viral entry. HIV-1 infection upregulates both c-MET transcript abundance and receptor phosphorylation in primary CD4+ T cells. Genetic knockout, knockdown, or pharmacological inhibition of c-MET in CD4+ T cells markedly reduced HIV-1 Gag protein expression, viral production, and infectivity. Integrative analyses using RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, and HIV-1 infection and entry assays revealed that c-MET disruption decreased cell-surface expression of the HIV-1 receptor CD4 and the coreceptor CXCR4, thereby limiting viral entry and subsequent infection. In addition, c-MET disruption attenuated activation of NF-κB, STAT1/3, and MAPK signaling pathways, which are critical regulators of HIV-1 gene expression. Together, these findings demonstrate that HIV-1 exploits HGF/c-MET signaling to coordinate entry receptor availability with intracellular signaling programs that support viral replication. Our study identifies a previously unrecognized host pathway required for efficient HIV-1 infection of primary CD4+ T cells and highlights HGF/c-MET signaling as a potential target for host-directed anti-HIV-1 therapeutic strategies.IMPORTANCEThe hepatocyte growth factor (HGF)/mesenchymal-epithelial transition factor (c-MET) signaling pathway is a well-established regulator of cell growth, survival, and migration and has been extensively studied as a therapeutic target in cancer. However, its role in HIV-1 infection has remained unknown. In this study, we found that c-MET enhances HIV-1 infection of primary CD4+ T cells by facilitating viral entry. We further demonstrate that HIV-1 replication enhances HGF-dependent c-MET phosphorylation, which is required for downstream signaling. Genetic ablation or pharmacologic inhibition of c-MET reduces HIV-1 entry by decreasing expression of viral entry receptors. Moreover, c-MET inhibition or knockout disrupts activation of cellular signaling pathways, including NF-κB, JAK/STAT, and p38 MAPK. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for HGF/c-MET signaling in HIV-1 pathogenesis and suggest that targeting c-MET may represent a novel host-directed strategy for HIV-1 intervention.

title: LncRNA FGD5-AS1 promotes M2 polarization of tumor-associated macrophages to facilitate the malignant phenotype of non-small cell lung cancer cells.
abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) take up a high proportion among immune cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME), and their M2- polarized phenotype has been implicated in promoting non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) development. Long non-coding RNA FGD5-AS1 (FGD5-AS1) is up-regulated within multiple tumor types, which has been shown to modulate both TAMs polarization and metabolic reprogramming. However, its exact mechanisms in NSCLC are largely unclear. This study aims to investigate whether FGD5-AS1 regulates M2 polarization of TAMs and thereby influences the malignant progression of NSCLC, as well as to explore the underlying molecular mechanisms. Human monocytic leukemia THP-1 cells were induced to differentiate into M0 macrophages in vitro and subsequently co-cultured with NSCLC cell lines (A549 and NCI-H1299) to mimic the TME and generate TAMs. The impacts of FGD5-AS1 silencing on M2 polarization of TAMs were assessed using flow cytometry and quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR). To investigate the molecular mechanism underlying FGD5-AS1-mediated regulation of M2 polarization, Wnt5a was overexpressed via lentiviral transduction in FGD5-AS1-silenced M0 macrophages, followed by evaluation of Wnt5a expression and M2 polarization status using flow cytometry, qRT-PCR, and Western blot analysis. Finally, FGD5-AS1-silenced M0 macrophages were subjected to co-culture using A549 as well as NCI-H1299 cells, and functional consequences of FGD5-AS1- regulated M2-polarized TAMs on NSCLC cell growth, invasion, migration, alongside epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) were evaluated using Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8), scratch, Transwell, and Western blotting assays. FGD5-AS1 showed remarkable up-regulation inside M2-polarized TAMs. FGD5-AS1 knockdown inhibited the M2 polarization of TAMs, as evidenced by down-regulated M2 macrophage marker levels including CD206, interleukin (IL)-10, transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), and CCL22, along with decreased Wnt5a protein levels. Mechanistically, overexpression of Wnt5a reversed the inhibitory effects of FGD5-AS1 silencing on M2 polarization, indicating that Wnt5a acts downstream of FGD5-AS1 in this regulatory axis. Notably, silencing FGD5-AS1 in M0 macrophages attenuated the proliferation, migration, invasion, and EMT of A549 and NCI-H1299 cells in the co-culture system, suggesting a functional role of FGD5-AS1-modulated TAMs in promoting malignant phenotypes of NSCLC cells. FGD5-AS1 may promote M2 polarization of TAMs through upregulation of Wnt5a, thereby contributing to the enhancement of malignant phenotypes in NSCLC cancer cells.

title: Inhibition of CDK1 attenuates cardiac remodeling via suppression of fibroblast-derived TGF-β1.
abstract: Activation of cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (CDK1) is implicated in fibrosis in liver and skin. However, the role of CDK1 in cardiac remodeling remains unclear. We investigated whether CDK1 inhibition suppresses cardiac remodeling and explored the underlying mechanisms. Angiotensin II (Ang II) was continuously infused into C57BL/6 mice with or without intraperitoneal administration of a selective CDK1 inhibitor (Ro-3306) for 1 week. Ro-3306 attenuated Ang II-induced increases in left ventricular wall thickness and heart weight without affecting blood pressure. Ro-3306 also ameliorated interstitial fibrosis and cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in Ang II-treated hearts, accompanied by reduced Col1a1 and Col3a1 mRNA expression. Ang II increased phosphorylation of CDK1 substrate motifs and transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) precursor protein levels, a key mediator of cardiac fibrosis and hypertrophy, and these were suppressed by Ro-3306. Ro-3306 also attenuated pressure overload-induced cardiac fibrosis and hypertrophy, accompanied by reduced TGF-β1 precursor protein levels. In cultured cardiac fibroblasts, inhibition of CDK1 by Ro-3306 or small interfering RNA suppressed Ang II-induced increases in TGF-β1 precursor protein levels, whereas no such effect was observed in cultured cardiomyocytes. In contrast, CDK2 knockdown or CDK4/6 inhibitors did not affect TGF-β1 precursor protein levels in cardiac fibroblasts. Comprehensive secretome analysis identified TGF-β1 as a major growth factor secreted from fibroblasts in response to Ang II. Conditioned medium from fibroblasts treated with Ang II induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy. CDK1 knockdown in fibroblasts suppressed TGF-β1 secretion. Neutralizing TGF-β1 antibodies attenuated hypertrophic effects of conditioned medium from fibroblasts treated with Ang II. In conclusion, CDK1 inhibition attenuates cardiac fibrosis and hypertrophy in vivo, accompanied by reduced cardiac TGF-β1 precursor protein levels. Our in vitro findings further suggest that CDK1 in cardiac fibroblasts regulates TGF-β1 production and secretion, thereby contributing to cardiomyocyte hypertrophy. KEYWORDS: CDK1 Cardiac fibrosis Cardiac hypertrophy TGF-β1.

title: Cross-omics mapping of the human HIV restrictome across clinical states, immune-cell compartments, and protein responses.
abstract: Host restriction factors can block HIV at multiple stages, but they are often studied as individual genes or within a single molecular layer. I performed an evidence-structured computational reanalysis of three independent public datasets to determine how the human HIV restrictome varies across clinical states, immune-cell compartments, and protein responses. The analysis used bulk monocyte RNA sequencing (GSE157198), PBMC single-cell/CITE-seq data (GSE256089), and primary CD4 T-cell proteomics (PXD012263) within a prespecified restrictome-immunometabolism framework. In GSE157198, ART-naive monocytes had higher core-restrictome activity than healthy controls (difference = 1.154, p = 0.000746), and core scores were strongly correlated with interferon/innate-sensing scores (Spearman r = 0.800, p = 7.47 × 10^-11). Core-lipid/cholesterol correlation was weaker and was not independent of interferon after conditional analysis. In GSE256089, participant-paired core-restrictome scores were enriched in NK cells relative to B cells, monocytes, and T cells, and matched random-gene-set analyses supported enrichment beyond background expression structure. FCGR3A monocytes also had higher participant-paired core scores than CD14 monocytes. Exploratory sensing/death-gene analysis identified cell-type-specific expression patterns but did not establish pathway activation, pyroptosis, or apoptosis. In PXD012263, the historical q < 0.05 proteomic selection contained 19 curated genes and retained mixed response polarity; sensitivity thresholds q < 0.01 and q < 0.10 selected 10 and 25 genes, respectively. Together, the results show that HIV restrictome activity varies across clinical and immune-cell contexts and is embedded within broader interferon-linked and immunometabolic states. Because the datasets are independent and not subject matched, the findings are observational and hypothesis-generating rather than causal.

title: A critical evaluation of Gene Ontology priors in biologically-informed neural networks
abstract: Biologically-informed neural networks (BINNs) embed prior knowledge such as the Gene Ontology (GO) into their architecture to produce interpretable representations, yet whether and how this prior improves performance or interpretation remains unclear. We introduce GONNECT, a BINN incorporating GO into an autoencoder. We evaluate GO constraints in the encoder, decoder, or both on RNA-seq tumour samples from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), comparing against published BINNs (OntoVAE, VEGA), an unconstrained baseline, randomized priors, and untrained networks. Across various performance metrics, GO structure adds little to reconstruction or latent-space organization, frequently matched by randomized or unconstrained models. Node activations agree with a gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)-derived reference, but this agreement largely arises from the architectural constraint: it is lost when GO connections are randomized, present even before training in the encoder, and learned in the decoder. Regularized soft links outside GO (GONNECT-SL) are unstable across runs and concentrate where the ontology is sparse, compensating for the prior's constraints rather than revealing new biology. Within this setting, we find no evidence that node activations capture biological information beyond that encoded by the predefined gene sets, suggesting that their apparent interpretability largely reflects the prior imposed by the architecture.

title: Modeling patient variants of Cnot1 and Cdc42bpb results in distinct forms of congenital diaphragmatic hernia in mice.
abstract: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a severe congenital anomaly characterized by impairment of both diaphragm and lung development in utero. CDH presents as a spectrum of forms and severities, with diaphragm defects arising in the dorsal/posterior region typically correlating with more severe pulmonary disease and higher risk of mortality than those appearing in ventral/anterior regions. The genetic etiology underlying CDH is complex, with many implicated genes showing variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance in both human patients and mouse models. Here we present in vivo validation of two genes previously unassociated with CDH: the CDC42-interacting kinase CDC42BPB; and CNOT1, a scaffolding protein of the CCR4-NOT protein complex, critical for mRNA regulation through modifications such as deadenylation. Each gene was found to have a damaging, de novo missense variant in a recent large-scale CDH patient sequencing screen. Loss of Cdc42bpb leads to ventral diaphragmatic hernias, heart septal defects, and minor lung epithelial differentiation defects in mouse embryos. Installation of the orthologous patient-specific missense variant through CRISPR/Cas9 editing leads to less severe ventral diaphragm defects. Mouse embryos with either one or two copies of the orthologous Cnot1 variant, c.1867C > T (p.R623W), develop dorsal diaphragmatic hernias with low (<50%) penetrance, and mutants showed alterations in mRNA isoform expression consistent with the molecular role of Cnot1 in RNA splicing. These results underscore the power of in vivo functional modeling to validate genes and patient-specific variants uncovered by patient sequencing, reveal two previously unrecognized genetic causes of CDH, and highlight the heterogeneity of different patient anatomic presentations.

title: Integrative long-read sequencing, RNA-seq and machine learning framework characterizes and predicts autosomal silencing in unbalanced X-autosome translocations.
abstract: X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) equalizes dosage between females (XX) and males (XY), yet its functional and clinical consequences remain challenging to interrogate in humans. Unbalanced X-autosome translocations constitute a natural model in which skewed inactivation of the derivative chromosome can spread into autosomes, contributing to phenotypic variability. Evaluating this spread and possible mediating factors is therefore essential for accurate clinical management. Using allele-resolved long-read sequencing and RNA sequencing, we investigated DNA methylation and gene expression across autosomal regions involved in unbalanced X-autosome translocations. We identified gene-level variability in autosomal silencing, marked by promoter hypermethylation, gene body hypomethylation, and reduced gene expression with clinical impact in affected individuals. Using epigenetic and genomic features around silenced and active autosomal genes reported here and in the literature, we developed an interpretable machine-learning model that identified intrinsic sequence and chromatin features associated with susceptibility or resistance to silencing. This framework enables discrimination between silenced and active autosomal genes and prioritization of clinically relevant genes. Our findings reveal principles underlying the variable spreading of XCI into autosomal genes, supporting a model in which intrinsic DNA sequences and chromatin features modulate the extent of XIST-mediated silencing and its clinical impacts.

title: Data-Driven Virus Discovery with Virushunter and Virusgatherer.
abstract: We present Virushunter and Virusgatherer, a bipartite computational workflow for discovering viral genomes from unprocessed next-generation sequencing data. Virushunter conducts a profile Hidden Markov Model-based sequence homology search for viral hallmark protein-coding sequence reads to construct microcontigs, which are used as seeds for targeted viral genome assembly by Virusgatherer. We showcase the application of Virushunter and Virusgatherer through an RNA virus-wide screen in 3348 bat transcriptome sequencing experiments from the Sequence Read Archive. Many of the discovered viruses are likely prototypes of new putative virus species, including a novel alphacoronavirus identified in a South American velvety free-tailed bat and a novel rhabdovirus in a European barbastelle bat. The tools are implemented as a reproducible Snakemake pipeline, which is available at https://github.com/lauberlab/VirusHunterGatherer.

title: Integrating Transcriptomic and Proteome Analysis to Understand Muscle Qualities and Related Regulatory Factors of Holstein Beef Under Transportation Stress.
abstract: This study aimed to explore the impact of transportation stress on beef quality and related regulatory mechanisms. Twelve Holstein steers of similar weight were divided into two groups: transportation for 15 h (STR) and transportation for 0 h (CON). The differences in meat quality, myofibril structure, and flavor components between transport-stressed and normal beef were compared. Through a comprehensive analysis of the transcriptome and proteome of the longissimus lumborum, the genes, proteins related to transport stress in meat were identified. The study found that the shear force, water loss rate, and drip loss of beef in the STR group were significantly higher than those in the CON group (p ≤ 0.05), and the marble grade of beef in the STR group was significantly lower than that in the CON group (p = 0.035); Muscle transmission electron microscopy, it was found that transportation significantly shortened the length of the sarcomere. Furthermore, long-distance transport has a detrimental effect on muscle flavor. We found that six DEGs/DEPs showed the same trend in mRNA and protein expression. It is plausible that transport stress influences beef quality and flavor, at least in part, through ferroptosis pathway-mediated lipid peroxidation. Meanwhile, the observed changes in stress-responsive genes/proteins (HMOX1 and BDH1) were linked to concomitant alterations in meat quality-associated genes/proteins (COL1A1, FMOD, and MYL3), indicating that these molecular events may collectively contribute to quality deterioration. Our results provide important insights into the impact of transportation stress on beef quality.

title: Stromal or exosome derived lncRNAs regulate stemness in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains one of the most prevalent malignancies worldwide, with high recurrence rates and chemotherapy resistance posing major clinical challenges. Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are recognized as an important contributors of HCC initiation, metastasis, and recurrence. Within the tumor microenvironment (TME), cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) can maintain CSC properties through intercellular communication. Exosomes serve as essential mediators of this process by delivering long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) from various TME cells (including CAFs, MSCs, macrophages, and HCC cells themselves) to recipient HCC cells. A literature search of PubMed and Web of Science Core Collection (inception to March 2026) was conducted using key terms including "HCC", "CAFs", "MSCs", "Macrophages", "Exosome", "LncRNA", and "Neoplastic Stem Cells". Studies were selected based on topic relevance and methodological rigor; those with incomplete or inaccessible data were excluded. The retrieved literature was synthesized to elucidate the mechanisms by which lncRNAs modulate downstream signaling pathways and to evaluate their translational potential as diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. This review identifies multiple mechanisms through which stromal or exosome derived lncRNAs regulate HCC cell stemness, including YAP liquid-liquid phase separation, chromatin remodeling via recruitment of SWI/SNF, INO80, NuRD, and BRM/BRG1 complexes, Wnt/β-catenin pathway modulation through protein stabilization and competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) networks, STAT3 pathway regulation via direct transcriptional repression and transcription factor recruitment, and BMP signaling pathway engagement. Functional classification reveals that these lncRNAs converge on core stemness pathways through complementary transcriptional, posttranscriptional, and protein-level regulatory mechanisms, while integrating signals from the TME. Stromal or exosome derived lncRNAs constitute a critical regulatory layer in HCC stemness maintenance and hold significant promise as noninvasive diagnostic biomarkers via liquid biopsy. Antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-based therapeutic strategies targeting the stromal cell-lncRNA-CSC axis represent a promising direction. Nevertheless, systematic characterization of stromal or exosome derived lncRNA species, elucidation of lncRNA sorting and uptake mechanisms, and clinical validation of biomarker and therapeutic applications remain important challenges for future investigation.

title: Telmisartan enhances anti-PD-1 efficacy in MSS colorectal cancer via modulation of PD-L1 and STAT3 signaling.
abstract: Microsatellite stable (MSS) colorectal cancer (CRC), accounting for over 85% of advanced cases, shows intrinsic resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors due to an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. The renin-angiotensin system (RAS), particularly angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1R), has been implicated in tumor progression and immune evasion. This study investigated whether telmisartan, a selective AT1R antagonist, modulates programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression and enhances anti-tumor immunity in MSS CRC. Mismatch repair (MMR) protein expression was characterized in human (SW480, HT29, HCT116) and murine (CT26) CRC cell lines. The effects of telmisartan on cell viability, PD-L1 expression, STAT3 signaling, and migration were evaluated using Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8), Western blotting, and Transwell assays. A CT26 tumor model in BALB/c mice was used to assess therapeutic efficacy alone or combined with pembrolizumab, with immunohistochemical analysis of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. Public transcriptomic analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) CRC data and immune infiltration analysis using the CIBERSORT (Cell-type Identification By Estimating Relative Subsets Of RNA Transcripts) algorithm were further performed. Telmisartan (10-20 μM) reduced PD-L1 expression in both MSS and MSI-H CRC cell lines without significant cytotoxicity. It was associated with increased signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) phosphorylation and reduced cell migration. In vivo, telmisartan inhibited tumor growth, while the combination with pembrolizumab resulted in enhanced antitumor efficacy. These effects were accompanied by increased infiltration of CD3⁺, CD4⁺, and CD8⁺ T cells. Transcriptomic analysis demonstrated positive correlations among AGTR1, STAT3, and CD274 expression, while CIBERSORT analysis revealed AGTR1-associated alterations in immune cell infiltration. Telmisartan may remodel the tumor immune microenvironment, potentially through modulation of PD-L1 expression associated with STAT3 signaling, thereby enhancing the response of MSS CRC to immune checkpoint blockade. These findings suggest that telmisartan could serve as a potential immunotherapy adjuvant for MSS CRC.

title: Elevational melanism in East African Honey Bees involves a Major-Effect locus.
abstract: Thermal melanism, whereby darker pigmentation occurs in colder environments, is a widespread pattern, yet its genetic and physiological basis in eusocial insects remains poorly understood. East African honey bees (Apis mellifera) occupy elevational gradients in which highland populations are darker, larger, and more cold tolerant than lowland conspecifics. Here, we integrated population genomics, structural variations, and functional genomics to investigate elevational melanism. We sampled, phenotyped and resequenced 139 workers from five East African mountain systems. A genome wide association study identified 977 Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) significantly associated with abdominal pigmentation, with a single, peak at the ebony ortholog AmEbony on chromosome 1. Allelic variation at AmEbony formed three genetic clusters tracking a continuous pigmentation gradient, and 77 divergent SNPs (DXY = 1) almost perfectly discriminated dark from light bees. Two inversions (r7, r9), previously linked to high elevation adaptation, were detected across additional mountain systems and enriched in dark, highland genomic backgrounds, but did not replace AmEbony as the primary pigmentation locus. CRISPR/Cas9 disruption of AmEbony in A. m. carnica produced darker adults in a qualitative comparison, supporting a conserved role in pigmentation. Head RNA-seq and GENIE3 analysis identified recurrent genotype-associated modules involving oxidoreductase activity and odorant binding. Because population structure covaries with elevation and pigmentation, the GWAS supports AmEbony as a major-effect locus but cannot identify causal variants. Similarly, head-expression data identify molecular changes associated with AmEbony disruption, but cannot establish whether they contribute to pigmentation or whether naturally segregating East African alleles act through the same pathways.

title: Beyond PROTACs: Conditional Technologies and New Frontiers.
abstract: This chapter surveys the post-PROTAC landscape of targeted protein degradation (TPD), covering conditional activation, new degradation modalities, and proximity-driven editing of post-translational modifications (PTMs). Condition-activated PROTACs harness prodrugs responsive to irradiation or the tumor microenvironment and nanoparticle-based platforms to achieve spatiotemporally resolved protein degradation. The targetable space is further expanded by molecular glues that recruit neosubstrates to E3 ligases, endocytosis-lysosome targeting chimeras that clear extracellular and membrane proteins, and autophagy-lysosome strategies that degrade aggregates and damaged organelles. Ribonuclease-recruiting chimeras achieve targeted RNA degradation, while the induced-proximity concept is repurposed for PTM regulation, enabling targeted glycosylation, acetylation, and phosphorylation and dephosphorylation via the recruitment of glycosyltransferases, acetyltransferases, and kinases and phosphatases. Future advances in all-small-molecule-based conditional systems, brain-targeted delivery, and regulatory frameworks informed by degradation kinetics will embed stimulus sensing and logic-gated operations into intelligent molecular systems, shifting the paradigm toward on-demand proteome and transcriptome rewiring for precision medicine.

title: Multiple Argonaute complexes orchestrate epigenetic silencing in the Arabidopsis germline.
abstract: Small RNAs (sRNAs) are widespread across diverse flowering plant species and play important roles regulating reproduction and environmental responses. However, how sRNAs exert their function is largely unknown, likely due to their typical origin in non-genic regions, the lack of distinct gene targets, and the sparse characterization of their associated Argonaute (AGO) effector proteins. Here we show that Arabidopsis male reproductive sRNAs associate with AGO4, 5, 6 and 9, all of which are enriched in meiocytes along with RNA Polymerase V (Pol V). This enables these sRNAs to methylate loci with imperfect sequence homology. AGO4, AGO6 and AGO9 predominantly load 24-nucleotide (nt) Pol IV-derived sRNAs and mediate DNA methylation in meiocytes in a dosage-dependent manner. Despite closer homology to microRNA-associated AGO1 and AGO10, AGO5 primarily binds CLSY3- and Pol IV-derived 21-24 nt sRNAs. Transcriptomic and methylomic analyses of meiocytes from single and compound ago mutants demonstrate distinct yet complementary roles of AGO4/6/9 and AGO5 in regulating protein-coding genes and silencing transposons in the germline. These molecular disruptions are accompanied by significant meiotic defects. Together, our findings reveal how AGO4/6/9-mediated DNA methylation and AGO5, likely acting through post-transcriptional gene silencing, work together to promote male germline development.

title: Identification photosynthesis-related genes in peanut (Arachis hypogaea L.) by hyperspectral phenomics, GWAS and RNA-seq.
abstract: Peanut (Arachis hypogaea L.) contributes importantly to the global food supply, and its yield potential is closely linked to leaf photosynthetic efficiency. However, conventional measurement of leaf net-photosynthetic-rate (Leaf Pn) is time- and labor-intensive, limiting its application to large breeding populations. We established a phenomics-driven framework integrating hyperspectral reflectance and genome-wide association studies for high-throughput evaluation and genetic dissection of Leaf Pn. Machine-learning models were trained on preprocessed spectral data from 1,200 leaf samples collected in four environments. Random forest performed best after Savitzky-Golay (S-G) smoothing and first-derivative transformation (R2 = 0.81, root mean square error [RMSE] = 1.50), outperforming the vegetation index-based model (R2 = 0.66). Applying this model to a panel of 173 peanut genotypes identified two quantitative trait loci, qPn5.1 and qPn13.1, encompassing seven candidate genes. Integrated analyses prioritized Arahy.K5L3ZW, which encodes protein kinase 2B. Silencing this gene increased Leaf Pn, whereas transient overexpression decreased it, indicating that Arahy.K5L3ZW negatively regulates Leaf Pn. This framework enables high-throughput genetic dissection of seedling photosynthetic capacity and identifies a candidate target for improving photosynthetic efficiency in peanut.

title: Glucosamine and selenium differentially regulate glutathione, lipid peroxidation, and mitochondrial function during glutamate stress in retinal neural cells.
abstract: Glutamate can disrupt cystine-dependent glutathione metabolism and promote oxidative and mitochondrial dysfunction in neural cells. We integrated human multiple-sclerosis optic-chiasm transcriptomics (GSE100297), glutamate-treated primary-neuron RNA sequencing (GSE255041), R28 differential-expression summaries, a normal human optic-nerve single-nucleus atlas (GSE236566), and R28 retinal precursor-cell experiments to characterize glucosamine (GlcN) and selenium responses. Human tissue showed enriched unfolded-protein-response, oxidative-stress, apoptosis, and ferroptosis programs, whereas glutamate-treated neurons predominantly exhibited amino-acid stress, unfolded-protein response, oxidative stress, and apoptosis, with weaker concordant ferroptosis enrichment. Glutamate reduced R28 metabolic activity, GSH/GSSG, and mitochondrial respiration and increased DCFH-DA and BODIPY-C11 oxidation. GlcN (2.5 mM) shifted the glutamate dose-response curve rightward and preserved GSH/GSSG and respiration, but lowered basal metabolic activity, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ATP-based viability. GlcN increased the LC3B-II/LC3B-I ratio, while changes in PCNA-normalized NRF2-related protein signals were modest. Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) partially restored respiration during glutamate exposure and was associated with higher ATP-based viability. RSL3 and erastin markedly reduced viability without glutamate; Fer-1 substantially restored viability, whereas GlcN did not. Selenium (1 μM) partially reduced RSL3-associated loss of viability without glutamate; the selenium-associated viability gain diminished during glutamate co-exposure (adjusted interaction P=0.0342). Selenium showed dose-dependent effects: 1 and 5 μM preserved metabolic activity, 5 μM reduced lipid oxidation, and 20 μM increased basal lipid oxidation. GlcN increased global O-GlcNAc modification approximately 3.6-fold and altered gp130 migration. In normal human optic nerve, redox/lipid-peroxidation programs were highest in myeloid cells, whereas hexosamine/O-GlcNAc capacity and SLC7A11 expression were prominent in astrocytic-stromal compartments. These findings identify distinct functional responses to GlcN and selenium within a mixed glutamate-stress phenotype that includes a ferrostatin-sensitive component. The GPX4 dependence of GlcN-mediated protection against glutamate remains unresolved.

title: Quantifying the impact of genetic mutations on enhancer dynamics.
abstract: Transcriptional regulation is mediated by enhancers, yet how genetic perturbations alter enhancer activity and gene expression remains unclear. We develop UDI-UMI-STARR-seq, integrating dual indexes and unique molecular identifiers, and combine it with RNA-seq to profile perturbation-associated changes in enhancer activity and gene expression. We apply this approach to 253,632 fragments representing 46,142 cell type-specific candidate enhancers and assess the impact of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of six transcription factors (ATF2, CTCF, FOXA1, LEF1, TCF7L2, and SCRT1). We identify responsive fragments that are repressed or induced and enriched for p53 family motifs. Enhancer-gene mapping reveals associations between responsive fragments and gene expression changes, including Wnt/p53 targets after ATF2 or LEF1 depletion. A deep learning model recapitulates enhancer grammar, including cooperative motif syntax and flanking sequence context. Applying this framework to 16p12.1 deletion identifies responsive fragments associated with genes involved in neuronal function, providing a scalable readout of enhancer dynamics across genetic perturbations.

title: TaSTG4B enhances wheat salt tolerance via regulation of antioxidant and photosynthetic protection pathways.
abstract: Soil salinization represents a major abiotic stress constraining wheat yield. Identifying key salt tolerance-related genes and unraveling their regulatory mechanisms is critical for breeding salt-tolerant wheat varieties. In this study, TaSTG4B (Triticum aestivum Salt-Tolerant Gene on 4B, gene ID: TraesCS4B02G042300), a key regulatory gene encoding an oxysterol-binding protein homolog, was jointly identified by ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)-induced mutagenesis screening and genome-wide association study (GWAS), and systematically elucidated its salt tolerance mechanisms. TaSTG4B exhibits relatively higher expression in wheat roots, suggesting that it primarily functions in this organ. Under 200 mM NaCl treatment (simulating moderate salt stress in saline-alkali soils), TaSTG4B overexpression (OE) lines exhibited significantly greater shoot and root biomass, and elevated activities of antioxidant enzymes compared to the wild type (Fielder). In contrast, TaSTG4B knockout (KO) lines showed markedly reduced salt tolerance. Physiological analysis revealed that TaSTG4B overexpression enhances wheat's antioxidant capacity, maintains ion homeostasis, and mitigates membrane damage under salt stress. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis revealed that under non-stress conditions, TaSTG4B primarily regulates pathways such as secondary metabolite biosynthesis-including key salt-stress-related pathways like proline (PRO), polyamine, and flavonoid biosynthesis-as well as glutathione metabolism, collectively establishing a "primed state of defense." Under salt stress, it activates glutathione metabolism, photosynthesis-antenna proteins, and ion homeostasis pathways, coordinating antioxidant defense and photosynthetic protection.
